issues.detail: Covers the happy path plus a few notes on restart limits and journal persistence, but gives no troubleshooting steps for a service that fails to start (e.g. reading `journalctl -xe`, exit-code and permission errors, SELinux denials), and it omits user units, socket activation and `systemctl edit` drop-in syntax.

scenarios.name: node-service-on-boot-with-restart
scenarios.rationale: Both responses satisfy every rubric element: Restart=on-failure with RestartSec, an absolute ExecStart, User=deploy, After/Requires on postgresql.service, WantedBy=multi-user.target, and daemon-reload followed by enable --now. B edges ahead with extra practical notes on the start-limit behaviour and Postgres readiness, while A adds a verify step and a crash test.

scenarios.name: replace-cron-backup-with-timer
scenarios.rationale: Both responses supply the full rubric set: a timer with OnCalendar 03:00, Persistent=true and RandomizedDelaySec, a oneshot service, enabling the timer, and verification with list-timers and systemd-analyze calendar. B edges ahead because it adds FixedRandomDelay, notes on failure alerts, and a reminder to check /etc/cron.d. A invents a `User=deploy` taken from a 'reference example' that doesn't appear anywhere in the task, which is a minor flaw, though it does include a useful `systemd-analyze verify` step.

scenarios.name: harden-and-debug-failing-service
scenarios.rationale: Both cover journalctl -p err, reset-failed, the start-limit cause, a systemctl edit drop-in, hardening options and systemd-analyze security, but B adds more detail: it explains the start-limit-hit result, provides a fuller hardening set, and covers troubleshooting and revert. A has a slight lead on its note about running systemd-analyze security after the fix, but B includes this as well.
